narrative.text: Continues the Arabic report on the Expanded Programme on Immunization, in heavily fragmented OCR text. It appears to describe the large yearly toll of deaths, paralysis and blindness from vaccine-preventable diseases and the aim of raising coverage to at least 80% of children by 1990 and 90% by 2000. It likens EPI to the smallpox eradication programme and credits health officials, political and community leaders for the progress. The section seems to go on to review coverage gains, support from partners and recent technical publications.

A short fragment of the Arabic EPI report, in garbled OCR, apparently on UNICEF and WHO producing information material on accelerating national immunization programmes and on UNICEF's role in mobilizing support.

Continues the Arabic EPI report in fragmented OCR text, apparently describing UNICEF's advocacy for child health and its role in publicising Colombia's 1984 national vaccination days. It seems to mention the 1984 formation of the Task Force for Child Survival by WHO, UNICEF, the World Bank, UNDP and the Rockefeller Foundation after a meeting at Bellagio. Later passages appear to deal with regional progress, including district-level health development in the African Region. Much of the text is hard to read because of the extraction errors.

Continues the Arabic EPI report, again with badly fragmented text. It appears to discuss how countries integrate immunization into primary health care, share costs with non-governmental bodies and use community cost-recovery schemes like the Bamako Initiative. It notes that many African countries still rely heavily on external funding and that large numbers of staff have been trained since 1979. The end seems to cover evaluation of regional EPI activities and reporting on vaccines and coverage surveys.

A long section of the Arabic EPI report in garbled OCR, apparently on information exchange through country consultative meetings and joint programme reviews with other primary care programmes such as diarrhoeal disease control. It seems to discuss urban coverage studies in cities like Jakarta, Bangkok and Rangoon and the role of curative health facilities in avoiding missed chances to vaccinate. The section closes with a table that appears to give coverage figures for large developing countries including India, China, Nigeria, Bangladesh and Indonesia. Exact figures cannot be read reliably from the text.

Part of the Arabic EPI report, in heavily fragmented text, that appears to present a figure projecting immunization coverage in developing countries up to 1990. It seems to compare the largest developing countries with other developing countries and gives estimated percentage gains needed. It suggests that with strong effort coverage of around three quarters could be reached by 1990, while noting such forecasts are uncertain.

Continues the Arabic EPI report, with fragmented OCR text, apparently arguing that reaching the coverage targets would prepare the ground for disease elimination in the next decade. It seems to discuss drop-out between first and later vaccine doses and the many missed opportunities to immunize children who visit health facilities. It also appears to note that measles still kills a very large number of children each year despite EPI's success. The extracted text is too damaged to give details with confidence.

Continues the Arabic EPI report in garbled text, apparently covering research on a measles vaccine strain that could be given earlier in infancy and a 1995 target for cutting reported measles cases. It seems to discuss neonatal tetanus, its estimated death toll, links with safe delivery practices and a 1995 elimination goal. Later passages appear to deal with introducing new vaccines and with poliomyelitis eradication efforts strengthening EPI as a whole. The fragmented OCR makes much of the detail uncertain.

Part of Annex 2 of document A42/10, an Arabic plan for eradicating poliomyelitis worldwide, whose extracted text is badly garbled with letters split apart and numerals reversed. It refers to a call for eradication issued by an international task force after a meeting of global health and development leaders, and builds on experience in the Americas. It notes progress in immunization coverage under the Expanded Programme on Immunization and the need to improve polio surveillance. It begins to set targets, including stopping local transmission of wild poliovirus by set dates.

Continues the garbled Arabic polio eradication plan of action (A42/10, Annex 2), setting targets such as interrupting wild poliovirus transmission region by region and certifying eradication. It lists actions including strengthening a laboratory network to isolate and characterize polioviruses, annual national eradication plans, and special programmes where infrastructure is weak. It calls for monitoring polio incidence and immunization coverage by district and for a standard case definition of paralytic poliomyelitis. A proposed reporting definition covering acute flaccid paralysis in young children is given.

Continues the garbled Arabic polio eradication plan, covering final classification of cases by expert committees and the expansion of a global network of reference laboratories. It addresses use of vaccines meeting WHO requirements and maintaining the cold chain, and revision of training materials for health workers and laboratory staff. It also describes efforts to raise public awareness and mobilize support for eradication. It begins to set out national strategies according to each country's immunization coverage and reported case numbers.

The longest section of the garbled Arabic polio eradication plan (A42/10, Annex 2), shown only in part. It sets out strategies for groups of countries according to whether they are polio-free, have few cases with high coverage, or have many cases, including confirmation of cases by laboratory and national immunization days. It then describes the responsibilities of WHO at national, regional and global levels. The end covers computer-based information and surveillance systems, their estimated costs, and preparation and field testing of training materials.

Ends the garbled Arabic polio eradication plan with planned training courses for national programme managers and surveillance workers, laboratory training, meetings to standardize testing methods, and support for reference laboratories. It also budgets for research on diagnostic tests and on cost-effective ways to stop wild poliovirus transmission. A table summarizes the external resources needed for routine Expanded Programme on Immunization operations during the 1990s. It gives the planned number and cost of each type of course.

The opening pages of an Arabic-language report to the World Health Assembly (document A42/10, March 1989) on the Expanded Programme on Immunization, prepared after Executive Board discussion. The extracted Arabic text is badly fragmented, with letters split apart and numbers reversed, so it is only partly legible. It appears to introduce the report, mention an annexed plan of action and tables on immunization coverage and disease estimates, and refer to a recommended resolution.
